title: Is It Better to Be Single Than in the Wrong Relationship?
paragraphs:
Is It Better to Be Single Than in the Wrong Relationship?
The Question That Breaks Hearts, Exposes Idols, and Reveals Why Waiting on Jesus Is Never Wasted
Some wounds don't begin with betrayal.
They begin with loneliness.
Not the loneliness of being alone—but the loneliness of watching everyone else seemingly find love while you keep wondering if God forgot your name.
You scroll through engagement photos.
Wedding videos.
Gender reveals.
Anniversary posts.
Happy family pictures.
Meanwhile...
You pray.
You wait.
You cry.
You wonder if saying "yes" to the wrong person would hurt less than hearing another quiet night in an empty room.
Maybe you've already been there.
Maybe you're there right now.
Maybe you're holding onto a relationship that God never asked you to keep because you're terrified that letting go means ending up alone forever.
But what if the greatest danger isn't singleness?
What if it's choosing companionship that slowly pulls your heart away from Christ?
That question isn't new.
God answered it thousands of years ago.
And His answer still rescues hearts today.
The Apostle Paul wrote words that many people misunderstand because they only read them through modern culture instead of through the historical and biblical context in which they were written.
In 1 Corinthians 7:8, Paul says:
"To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am."
The Greek reads:

καλὸν αὐτοῖς ἐὰν μείνωσιν ὡς κἀγώ
(kalon autois ean meinōsin hōs kagō)
The word καλόν (kalon) does not merely mean "acceptable."
It carries the sense of something beautiful, honorable, beneficial, fitting, and good according to God's purposes.
Paul is not declaring singleness spiritually superior.
He is declaring that singleness is not a curse.
It is not God's leftover plan.
It is not second place.
It can be a beautiful calling that allows undivided devotion to Christ.
Just a few verses later he explains why.

In 1 Corinthians 7:32–35, Paul says that the unmarried believer can be concerned with "the things of the Lord," while the married person must also care for the responsibilities of marriage. He makes clear he is not laying down a command but offering wise counsel for wholehearted devotion to God.
That completely changes the conversation.
The Bible never teaches:
"Find someone at any cost."
The Bible teaches:
"Seek first the kingdom of God."
Jesus Himself said in Matthew 6:33:
"But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you."
The Greek begins:

ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον
(zēteite de prōton)
The word πρῶτον (prōton) means "first," "before everything else," "highest priority."
Not romance first.
Not marriage first.
Not emotional security first.
Christ first.
Always.
Because whenever we place someone else where only Jesus belongs...
we don't create love.
We create an idol.
The Old Testament reveals this same principle in language rich with covenant meaning.
In Psalm 27:14, David writes:
The Hebrew says:

קַוֵּה אֶל־יְהוָה
(qavveh el-YHWH)
The verb קַוָּה (qavah) means far more than passive waiting.
It carries the idea of hopeful expectation, eager trust, and being bound together like tightly twisted cords.
Biblical waiting is not sitting still while life passes by.
It is wrapping your hope so tightly around God that disappointment cannot pull it apart.
Our culture says:
"You're incomplete until someone loves you."
Jesus says:
"You are complete in Me."
Paul echoes this in Colossians 2:10:
"And you have been filled in Him."
Our identity begins in Christ, not in relationship status.
That truth matters because the wrong relationship often begins with the right desire pursued in the wrong direction.
Wanting marriage is not sinful.
Wanting companionship is not sinful.
Wanting children is not sinful.
God Himself declared in Genesis 2:18:
"It is not good that the man should be alone."
Marriage is God's gift.
But gifts become dangerous when they replace the Giver.
Scripture repeatedly warns believers against relationships that draw them away from wholehearted faithfulness to God.
For example, 2 Corinthians 6:14 says:
"Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers."

The Greek phrase μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (mē ginesthe heterozygountes) pictures two different animals forced under the same yoke, pulling in different directions. While this passage has a broader application than marriage alone, it certainly speaks to partnerships that fundamentally oppose a believer's devotion to Christ. The issue is not human worth—every person bears God's image—but spiritual direction and covenant faithfulness.
History is filled with people who ignored that warning.
King Solomon began with wisdom.
He ended with divided worship because his heart followed after other gods through relationships that drew him away from the Lord (1 Kings 11).
Samson possessed extraordinary strength.
Yet repeated compromise in relationships led to devastating consequences (Judges 13–16).
These accounts are not merely ancient history.
They are mirrors.
Sometimes the greatest heartbreak isn't the breakup.
It's slowly becoming someone you never wanted to become because you loved someone who didn't love the God you serve.
The wrong relationship can slowly convince you that compromise is maturity.
That silence is peace.
That disobedience is love.
But biblical love never asks us to abandon obedience to Christ.
Jesus never called us to lose ourselves in another person.
He called us to deny ourselves and follow Him (Mark 8:34).
Those are not the same thing.
If someone consistently pulls you away from prayer...
from Scripture...
from holiness...
from the fellowship of believers...
from integrity...
from worship...
you may not be protecting love.
You may be protecting the very thing keeping you from experiencing God's best.
That realization can feel devastating.
Because letting go often feels like dying.
In some ways, it is.
Dreams die.
Plans die.
Imagined futures die.
But throughout Scripture, God has always been in the business of bringing resurrection where people only see endings.
The cross looked like defeat.
The empty tomb revealed it was redemption all along.
That is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
It is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The greatest scandal in history was not simply humanity's rebellion.
It was that the sinless Son of God willingly bore our shame.
Isaiah prophesied:
"He was pierced for our transgressions."
The innocent took the place of the guilty.
The Holy One carried the scandal we deserved.
Then grace wrote the final chapter.
That same Savior still rewrites stories today.
Perhaps your story includes divorce.
Perhaps betrayal.
Perhaps abuse.
Perhaps years spent waiting.
Perhaps regrets over relationships you wish had never happened.
None of those chapters have the authority to become your final chapter if your life belongs to Christ.
The Gospel never minimizes sin.
It magnifies grace.
Not cheap grace that ignores repentance.
Saving grace that transforms repentant sinners into new creations.
Jesus does not merely repair broken hearts.
He creates new hearts.
The prophet Ezekiel records God's promise:
"I will give you a new heart."
God specializes in what seems impossible.
Maybe today you feel forgotten because no one has chosen you.
But Calvary declares that you have already been chosen by the One whose love never fails.
Human love says,
"I'll stay as long as you're enough."
Jesus says,
"I loved you while you were still a sinner."
Human relationships often depend on performance.
Christ's covenant rests on His finished work at the cross.
That does not mean marriage is unimportant.
Far from it.

Biblical marriage beautifully reflects Christ's covenant love for His Church (Ephesians 5:25–32). Yet because it reflects something so sacred, it should never be entered carelessly or contrary to God's wisdom.
It is far better to wait faithfully than to rush toward a relationship that slowly distances you from the Savior who gave everything for you.
If your waiting is leading you closer to Christ...
it is never wasted.
If your singleness is producing deeper holiness...
it is never empty.
If your tears are driving you to Jesus...
they are watering ground where faith can grow.
Perhaps today your greatest prayer should not be,
"Lord, send me someone."
Perhaps it should become,
"Lord, make me more like Your Son."
Because the safest heart to entrust to another person is one already surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Sometimes one faithful share becomes the conversation God uses to redirect a life toward Christ.
One surrendered heart today may become the testimony someone else desperately needs tomorrow.
